summary: NEXUS_5 is an interactive Martian surface navigation and survival interface designed to assist astronauts during Extravehicular Activities (EVAs). Raw orbital datasets from Mars satellites are dense and difficult to interpret in real time during high-stakes field operations. NEXUS_5 solves this operational bottleneck by translating complex orbital telemetry into an intuitive, live heads-up interface. Beyond standard topographic terrain maps, the platform displays real-time surface temperature, oxygen levels, atmospheric pressure, average thermal conditions, and active weather patterns directly linked to orbital satellite uplinks. Inspired by proven Earth-based telemetry systems used by mountain rescue teams and wildfire first responders, NEXUS_5 tracks critical resource thresholds and environmental hazards. If an astronaut navigates toward a zone with lethal atmospheric or terrain conditions, the system triggers an immediate "Do Not Step Foot" warning to protect crew safety.
details:
NEXUS_5 transforms dense, Earth-processed orbital satellite datasets into a fast, life-critical interface for astronauts conducting Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) on Mars. Rather than relying on static 2D maps or raw satellite imagery, NEXUS_5 connects directly to an orbital satellite uplink pipeline to render real-time environmental telemetry over the Martian terrain. The interface tracks live and average surface temperature, ambient and suit oxygen levels, atmospheric barometric pressure, and live weather events such as dust storms and high winds. When an astronaut's route approaches an area with dangerous terrain or lethal atmospheric readings, NEXUS_5 automatically triggers a "Do Not Step Foot" hazard protocol to prevent them from entering the zone.

Benefits & Intended Impact During surface exploration, astronauts have limited time, oxygen, and battery reserves to manually analyze complex data. NEXUS_5 reduces cognitive load and eliminates blind footsteps in hostile environments, directly improving crew survivability and mission efficiency on Mars and future planetary frontiers.

Inspiration & Design Considerations Our design draws directly from field-tested navigation tools used by wildfire firefighters and mountain rescue responders on Earth. When navigating rugged cliffs or active fire lines, first responders rely on maps that simultaneously display steep terrain obstacles alongside remaining oxygen and battery limits. We adapted this exact survival framework for Martian EVA operations, prioritizing high-contrast visual alerts, rapid readability, and proactive hazard warnings.

Tools & Development We conceptualized the interface architecture using NASA Mars orbital mapping datasets, structured our system pipeline in Microsoft Word, and developed the visual demonstration slides using Google Gemini and Google
